newsitem.title: USA: Millon Air has no immediate comment on crash.
newsitem.headline: Millon Air has no immediate comment on crash.

text.p: Millon Air officials had no immediate comment Wednesday on the crash of their Boeing Co 707 aircraft in Ecuador Tuesday night.
"Everyone here is too busy to talk," said a Millon employee who answered the phone and declined to give his name.
Earlier an employee said a statement would be issued around 1015 EDT/1415 GMT, but the employee said it was unlikely the company would have a statement until after 1400 EDT/1800 GMT.
The Millon flight crashed into Manta, a residential area 290 miles south of Quito, killing the crew members and at least 20 people on the ground.

Millon, which traditionally shuns any press coverage, is a family-run business. It flies charters as well as some scheduled flights from Miami to many destinations in Latin America, said industry sources.

The Boeing 707 model that crashed is considered a reliable workhorse in the cargo industry. The B707, however, is relatively expensive to operate because it burns a lot of fuel and requires much maintenance because of its age.
The flight was carrying fresh flowers and fish.

The accident was not the first involving a Millon plane in Latin America in recent years. On April 28, 1995, a Millon Air McDonnell-Douglas DC-8 overran a runway into a shantytown area in Guatemala City, Guatemala, killing at least six people on the ground, injuring the aircraft's three crewmembers and destroying the plane.

And in February, a Millon 707 headed into Miami International Airport had a problem with its landing gear and skidded to a stop without its landing equipment. There were no injuries in the MIA incident.
Millon carried the seventh most international freight throuh Miami International Airport in 1995, hauling 50,759 tons, according to statistics compiled by the Dade County Aviation Department.
